analysis.one_liner: Bans clearcutting and commercial logging in old-growth and roadless federal forests.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in August 2002 and received no hearing, markup, or vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would ban clearcutting and other even-age logging on National Forest, Bureau of Land Management, and National Wildlife Refuge land, and would prohibit logging and new road construction in old-growth forests, roadless areas, streamside buffer zones, and dozens of named 'special areas' across 26 states. It would replace clearcutting with less destructive 'selection' logging where timber cutting continues, and would let ordinary citizens sue to enforce the rules, including against the federal government itself.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use public forests for recreation, drinking water, hunting, fishing, and wildlife, plus communities whose fishing, tourism, and guiding economies depend on intact forests. The bill's own findings argue that logging damage to streams and habitat has already cost jobs in fishing, hunting, tourism, and recreation [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Forest users, downstream communities, outdoor industries

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits clearcutting and other even-age logging on National Forest System land, federal land under the Bureau of Land Management, and National Wildlife Refuge System land, requiring a shift to selection logging or restoration where cutting continues [S2][S3].

Bans extractive logging and new road construction in ancient forests, roadless areas, watershed protection areas, and specially designated areas in 26 states, which protects drinking water sources, wildlife habitat, and recreation [S2][S3].

Gives any citizen the right to sue violators, including the United States, with a minimum $5,000 damage award and attorney's fees, and waives federal sovereign immunity, making the logging rules enforceable rather than advisory [S3].

Declares that selection logging is more job-intensive than clearcutting for the same timber output and produces higher-quality sawlogs, and its findings state that destruction of large natural forests has cost jobs in fishing, hunting, tourism, recreation, and guiding [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry, which would lose much of its access to federal timber — particularly old-growth and roadless stands — and road-building contractors who build logging roads on federal land. Timber-dependent mill towns in logging regions would face reduced federal timber supply.

drawbacks.text: The bill would remove a large share of federal timber from harvest, which would reduce supply for mills and logging jobs in timber-dependent communities — the standard objection to forest-protection legislation, acknowledged implicitly by the bill's own argument that selection logging is more labor-intensive per unit of timber [S3].

The citizen-suit provisions allow any person to sue for a minimum $5,000 statutory award with no notice requirement and de novo trials, which would invite a heavy volume of litigation against both private operators and the Forest Service, and the United States would pay damages out of the Treasury when it loses [S3].

Because it names specific tracts of land in statute, future land-management decisions for those areas would be frozen in law rather than worked out through the normal forest-planning process, even as conditions on the ground change [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main public benefit — protecting old-growth forests, roadless areas, and watersheds that are nearly all on federal land, with the bill noting that less than 10 percent of original unlogged US forest remains — is substantial and permanent, and the enforcement teeth would make the protections real. The main costs fall on a concentrated industry: timber companies lose federal timber supply and mill communities feel it. The citizen-suit machinery is unusually aggressive (minimum damages, no notice, waiver of sovereign immunity) and would generate litigation that even supporters would have to defend. On balance it is a strong conservation bill whose costs are borne by one industry and whose benefits are broadly public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on August 1, 2002, read twice, and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2003 — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Torricelli introduced the bill on August 1, 2002, joined by six other Senate Democrats: Kerry, Cleland, Reed, Corzine, Schumer, and Durbin [S3].
Six Democratic senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Senate referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the day it was introduced; the action history shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the 107th Congress [S5].
The bill never reached the Senate floor and never received a vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber industry kept its access to federal timber, including old-growth and roadless stands, and logging-road contractors kept their business — while the public gained nothing, since the protections were never enacted.

for.name: Sen. Robert Torricelli
for.role: Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Act to Save America's Forests on August 1, 2002 [S3][S5].

for.name: 6 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none became law [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 1, 2002 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote reported — before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Senate Democrat (7 introducers plus cosponsors, none Republican); the bill never reached a vote, so any partisan split beyond sponsorship is unrecorded [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill bans clearcutting and other even-age logging on federal land and ends extractive logging entirely in old-growth, roadless, and specially designated forests, cutting off much of the industry's federal timber supply. Its interest in continued federal harvests runs against the public benefits of intact watersheds, wildlife, and recreation the bill was written to protect [S2][S3].
The bill prohibits construction or reconstruction of roads in protected areas, eliminating road-building work tied to federal timber sales [S3].

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation, tourism, hunting and fishing businesses
industries.note: The bill's findings state that destruction of large natural forests has cost jobs in fishing, hunting, tourism, recreation, and guiding, and that clearcutting depletes sport and commercial fisheries; protecting unlogged forest would support those industries [S3].
